questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: I was motivated by a a strong desire to become more fluent in the language

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Murcia because it is a less known city, and I wanted to visit a new place rather than a city I had already been to

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found it challenging to get the information I needed. I was frustrated that my courses overlapped, which meant I had to choose new ones that needed approval from different places. Fortunately, they were quickly approved by my university in Denmark, but in Spain it took a bit longer. My university was also relocated to another place, and it was difficult to figure out where the different courses were held.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I contacted my advisor here in Murcia whenever I needed help. Unfortunately, she didn’t respond to my emails quickly, and there were times when she couldn’t provide answers to my questions either.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found my accommodation through Spotahome. There weren’t many options left when I was looking, so I recommend starting your search early and also checking the condition of the apartment.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Future exchange students should know that living off campus requires more planning and independence. It’s important to start searching for accommodation early, as options can be limited closer to the start of the semester. Always check the location in relation to the university and public transport. Also, make sure to read rental contracts carefully and check the condition of the apartment before moving in. Living off campus can offer more freedom and privacy, but it also means you’ll need to manage bills, landlords, and possibly roommates on your own.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I felt that it took quite some time, as I had to choose new courses 2–3 times due to scheduling conflicts, and you have to figure out the course overlaps yourself. That made the registration process longer and delayed getting access to their website. I also felt behind in school because I didn’t have access to the course materials, as I wasn’t registered yet.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I don't remember, but remember to check your emails

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can get help from your advisor, and there is also an Erasmus office where staff are available to assist Erasmus students.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Apart from the 2–3 times where there were scheduling conflicts, I managed to get into some good courses

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would advise future exchange students to start the registration process as early as possible and carefully check for any course overlaps themselves, as these are not flagged automatically. Be prepared to make changes and stay in close contact with your advisor. Don’t hesitate to reach out to the Erasmus office for help – they can guide you through the process if it becomes complicated. I would also recommend choosing the course 'Español de América' it was interesting and educational, easy to follow, and very popular among Erasmus students.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some courses were more difficult than others. The ones labeled “optativa” were easy, while the ones labeled “obligatoria” were more difficult.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teacher talks a lot and the students talk less. Many of the teachers use PowerPoint, but I had one teacher who didn’t use any materials at all, so you had to be good at taking notes in his class (he teaches the course 'Perspectivas actuales de la lingüística'). Sometimes they give assignments, both group and individual. Some teachers require that assignments be handwritten on blank paper using a pen. Some classes are called 'práctica' – these are sessions you must attend to earn good points toward your final grade. A paper is handed out where you have to sign to confirm your attendance. Some teachers, not all, might also give small in-class tests from time to time.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Español de America (Do yourself a favor and choose this course)
- Perspectivas actuales de la lingüística
- Literatura española. Narrativa
- Teoría de la literatura y literatura comparada
- América, sociedades de frontera: cultura e identidad (This course is from a different bachelor's program, not one under 'Lengua y Literatura Española'. I had to choose it because my other preferred courses overlapped, but I ended up loving it. However, the teacher sometimes gives a short test at the end of a topic, which counts for 1 point)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Español de América!!!!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: An unexpected expense was probably that, in addition to the €220 I had to pay for the apartment each month, the landlord asked me to pay an extra €100 for utilities that is, for water, electricity, and internet.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: non

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: An organization called ESN organizes various activities in Murcia that you can take part in. They even organized a trip to Ibiza. You can follow them on Instagram their handle is @esnmurcia. Another website that also offers activities is murciawelcomesyou. In Spain, they use the app WhatsApp a lot, so make sure to have it downloaded.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to parties that's where you meet people and other Erasmus students. Also, go to the festivals in Murcia there's always something happening out on the streets.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recommend that you also travel to other cities, such as Alicante, Cartagena, and Mazarrón, because it can get a bit boring to stay only in Murcia for five months

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I have been on exchange before, so I wasn’t very surprised.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just jump into it, be talkative the other Erasmus students are on exchange just like you and are easy to talk to.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They eat late in Spain, which I found challenging, and the shops are closed on Sundays.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The streets stay lively late into the night, especially during festivals, when everyone comes out to watch, celebrate, and take part in the atmosphere.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Practice writing by hand and memorizing, because during exams you write on paper by hand and without any aids.
2. There can be long breaks between your classes for example, you might have a class from 8-10, and then your next class doesn’t start until 15-17
3. There are usually classes in the evening

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
- Buy water from the supermarkets, as the tap water isn’t clean (that’s what my roommates told me)
- Always carry cash with you, you never know when something might happen, like a power outage, and you’re left without anything to eat (this happened to me during a blackout in Spain in 2025).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: What I found most rewarding was that my roommates didn’t speak English, so we only spoke Spanish it really helped improve my Spanish skills.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: My biggest challenge was probably when there was a fire hazard in my apartment. I was living in an old apartment where not everything was in good condition, and the fire department told us we couldn’t sleep there that night. I had to find a hotel on the same night.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
